bib.title: Combinatorial Bandits (Chapter 30, Bandit Algorithms)
bib.venue: Bandit Algorithms, Cambridge University Press (book chapter, pp. 362-377)

question: How can a learner with a combinatorial (binary hypercube) action set achieve low adversarial regret computationally efficiently under bandit and semi-bandit feedback?
contributions: Mirror descent with negentropy for semi-bandits (Alg 18, Thm 30.2)
FTPL with geometric-resampling estimator, one oracle call per round (Alg 19, Thm 30.4), shown as mirror descent

results.claim: Semi-bandit online stochastic mirror descent with unnormalised negentropy has regret sqrt(2nmd(1+log(d/m))) (Thm 30.2).
results.setup: Adversarial combinatorial bandit, action set A in {0,1}^d with at most m ones, losses y_t in [0,1]^d, regret R_n over n rounds. Semi-bandit feedback, eta = sqrt(2m(1+log(d/m))/(nd)).

results.claim: FTPL for semi-bandits with Laplace-style perturbation (density 2^-d exp(-||z||_1)) has regret m*sqrt(2(1+e^2)nd(1+log d)), needing eta*m >= 1.
results.setup: Adversarial combinatorial bandit, action set A in {0,1}^d with at most m ones, losses y_t in [0,1]^d, regret R_n over n rounds. Semi-bandit feedback; eta=sqrt(2(1+log d)/((1+e^2)dnm)), beta=ceil(1/(eta m)).
results.quote: its regret is bounded by Rn ≤m

results.claim: Exp3 for linear bandits applied with bandit feedback gives regret 2m*sqrt(3dn log|A|), an extra factor m over the standard linear bandit bound.
results.setup: Adversarial combinatorial bandit, action set A in {0,1}^d with at most m ones, losses y_t in [0,1]^d, regret R_n over n rounds. Bandit feedback (only <A_t,y_t> seen).
results.quote: which increases the regret by a factor of m

results.claim: Bandit-feedback bound has m^{3/2} dependence, and it is now known to be tight (Cohen et al. 2017).
results.quote: the lower bound was increased to show the upper bound is tight

results.claim: Semi-bandit worst-case lower bound is Omega(sqrt(dnm)), for large n and m <= d/2, matched up to constants by mirror descent with a different potential.

results.claim: FTPL replaces the unknown 1/P_ti with a geometric random variable K_ti with mean 1/P_ti, so the estimator needs no closed form probability: Yhat_ti = min(beta,K_ti) A_ti y_ti.
FTPL costs O(nd) expected oracle calls over n rounds, and O(beta n d) worst case if sampling of K_ti is truncated at beta.

results.claim: Exp3 and mirror descent are computationally intractable for general A: a repeated travelling salesman is a combinatorial bandit, and an efficient O(n^p), p<1 regret learner would approximate it.
results.quote: The combinatorial bandit can model a repeated version of the travelling salesman problem

results.claim: For m-sets the Hessian off-diagonals are non-positive, improving m-dependence to sqrt(m); FTPL would reach Otilde(sqrt(mnd)) (exercise, no source stated).
results.setup: A = {a in {0,1}^d: ||a||_1 = m}; fails for general sets (shortest path counterexample, Ex 30.10).

results.claim: Expected max of d iid Laplace-type coordinates equals the harmonic sum, E||Z||_inf = sum_{i=1}^d 1/i <= 1+log d.

limits: Efficient algorithm only for semi-bandit feedback; no general FTPL result for bandit feedback (Note 3).
Mirror descent and Exp3 are computationally intractable in general (TSP argument); efficiency depends on the action set and must be checked case by case.
FTPL requires an exact (or approximate) linear optimisation oracle for argmin_a <a,y>.
Stochastic setting only discussed in notes; no experiments, only regret bounds.
practices: Use semi-bandit feedback (observe per-coordinate losses of chosen components) when available; it removes the m^{3/2} penalty of bandit feedback (Sec 30.4, Note 1).

If an offline linear optimisation oracle exists, run FTPL: sample Z_t, play argmax <a, Z_t - eta*Lhat_{t-1}>, observe chosen coordinates, estimate each with a geometric sample truncated at beta (Alg 19).
Truncate geometric sampling at beta to bound worst-case oracle calls to O(beta n d) (Note 2).
For multi-task (sum-only feedback) with per-task losses observed, apply Exp3/Exp3-IX independently to each bandit (Sec 30.2).
For shortest path with semi-bandit feedback, play Exp3 over paths via the Takimoto-Warmuth / Gyorgy et al. weight-pushing approach for polynomial computation (Ex 30.3).

terms.definition: A combinatorial bandit is a linear bandit with an action set that is a subset of the d-dimensional binary hypercube
the vector (At1yt1, . . . , Atdytd); equivalent to observing yti for all i for which Ati = 1
edges d=|E|, path a in {0,1}^d with a_i=1 if edge i on path; loss <a,y_t>; m = length of longest path. Fig 30.1: bandit sees total travel time (21 h), semi-bandit sees each flight (1,12,8 h)
choose m of d ads, A_t with ||A_t||_1=m, loss <A_t,y_t>; order plays no role
d=mk coordinates partitioned into m parts; pick exactly one coordinate per part; only the aggregate loss is seen
A_t = argmin_a <a, eta*Lhat_{t-1} - Z_t>, Z_t from perturbation distribution Q
